misconceptions.say: On the squared one: try $x = -1$ and $y = 1$. Both have the same square, so the distance between two *different* points comes out as zero — and the second axiom is an if-and-only-if.
On the last one: read it again with the two points swapped. The definition treats $x < y$ and $x > y$ differently, and an axiom says it must not.

feedback.nudge: For each line, try to break it before trying to prove it. Three of the five are standard metrics you will meet again; the other two each fail exactly one axiom, and in both cases a pair of small numbers shows it.

distractors.0: Yes — the usual metric on the line. The triangle inequality is the ordinary one for absolute values.
distractors.1: Yes — the **discrete metric**. Every axiom holds trivially except the triangle inequality, and that holds because the left side is at most 1 while the right side is 0 only when both terms are, which forces $x = y = z$.
distractors.2: No. $d(-1, 1) = |1 - 1| = 0$ with $-1 \ne 1$, so axiom 2 fails. It is a pseudometric.
distractors.3: Yes — the **taxicab** (or $\ell^1$) metric. Each coordinate satisfies the triangle inequality and the sum of the inequalities is the inequality for the sum.
distractors.4: No. $d(0,1) = 1$ but $d(1,0) = 2$, so it is not symmetric. (It is a *quasi-metric*, and they do get used — for one-way streets.)

explanation:
## The three that work

**$|x-y|$ on $\R$** is the one everything else is measured against.

**The discrete metric** is the one that makes every intuition about distance useless, which is exactly why it is the first place to test a claim. Every point is at distance 1 from every other, so every set is open, every set is closed, and the only convergent sequences are eventually constant.

**The taxicab metric** on $\R^2$ adds the coordinate distances instead of taking the hypotenuse. It is a genuinely different metric — the balls are diamonds, not discs — but it is *equivalent* to the Euclidean one in the technical sense: the same sets are open.

## The two that fail, and how they fail

$|x^2 - y^2|$ fails the **identity of indiscernibles**, and only that half of it. $d(-1,1) = 0$ with $-1 \ne 1$. This is the standard shape of the mistake: a function that measures something *about* the points rather than the points themselves, and then cannot tell apart two points that agree on it.

The asymmetric one fails **symmetry** by construction. Worth noticing that it satisfies the other three, which is why quasi-metrics are a real object and not just a broken definition.

## The habit

Try to break it first. Four axioms is four proofs; one counterexample is one line.
